title: Relationship Slump: Signs, Causes and What to Do — cv.cm
description: Relationship slump or falling out of love? Signs, causes, a table to tell them apart, a 4-week plan to feel close again, and when to try counselling.
h1: What is a relationship slump and how do you get out of it?
answer: A relationship slump is a period when a relationship feels flat, routine or boring, usually after the exciting early phase fades. It is common and often temporary. Couples get through it by trying new things together, showing appreciation again, talking openly about the feeling, and giving each person time for their own life. If respect and care are gone, it may be more than a slump.

body: In Chinese and Japanese the word is 倦怠期, in Japanese also マンネリ, in Korean 권태기. In English people say a relationship slump, a rut, or "the honeymoon phase is over". It describes the same thing: you still care about your partner, but things feel flat. Dates feel the same, conversations are about chores, and the excitement of the beginning is gone.

This is a normal part of long relationships. In the early months, everything about the other person is new. Over time, novelty fades and life fills with work, study, money and family duties. A slump often appears after a year or two, after moving in together, after a baby, or during a stressful period. There is no fixed timeline.
A slump is not a sign that you chose the wrong person. It is a sign that the relationship needs attention.
Signs that you may be in a slump:

ul: Most conversations are about logistics: bills, dinner, who picks up whom.
You spend evenings on separate phones in the same room.
You have stopped going on dates or doing new things together.
Small habits of your partner annoy you more than before.
You feel less physical affection or desire.
You think less about your partner during the day.
Routine: doing the same few things every week.
Stress from outside, such as work, exams, money or caring for family, leaving no energy for each other.
Small hurts that were never talked about and slowly build distance.
Taking each other for granted: no more thanks, compliments or questions.
Losing your own life: friends, hobbies and goals, so you have less to bring to the relationship.

sections.h: Slump or falling out of love?
body: Many people in a slump worry that the love is gone. These are different situations, and it helps to look honestly at which one fits.

head: Question
More like a slump
More like falling out of love
rows: Do you still respect your partner?
Yes, you admire them even if you are bored
You often feel contempt or look down on them
When something good happens, who do you want to tell?
Still your partner, usually
Someone else, and you avoid telling them
Can you imagine a good future together?
Yes, if things felt closer
No, or you feel relief imagining life without them
Do you want to fix it?
Yes, you miss how it was
You feel you do not care either way
When you do something new together, how does it feel?
Better, closer for a while
Still empty or uncomfortable
How do conflicts go?
Few fights, mostly distance
Fights end badly, or you no longer bother to fight

body: If most answers are in the middle column, the relationship probably has a good base and needs effort. If most are in the right column, it is worth thinking seriously about what you want, perhaps with a counsellor. See cv.cm's article on whether you should get back together, which covers how to make big relationship decisions calmly.

A well-known set of studies by Arthur Aron and colleagues found that couples who took part in novel and exciting activities together reported higher relationship quality than couples who did only pleasant, familiar ones. The idea is simple: when you share something new, some of the excitement becomes linked to your partner again.

The Gottman Institute's research points to small daily moments too. Partners make "bids for connection" (a comment, a joke, a request), and couples who stay together turn toward those bids much more often than couples who split up. In a slump, many bids are missed because both people are tired or distracted. Noticing and answering them is one of the cheapest ways to feel close again.

Research by Shelly Gable and colleagues also found that how you respond to your partner's good news matters. Responding with real interest and joy ("That's amazing, tell me everything!") was linked with better relationships than a flat "nice" or changing the subject.

sections.h: A 4-week plan to get out of a slump

head: Week
Focus
What to do
rows: Week 1
Talk about it
Pick a calm time and say it gently: "I miss how close we used to feel. I'd like us to try some new things together. How do you feel about us lately?" Listen without blaming.
Week 2
Appreciation
Each day, say one specific thing you appreciate: "Thanks for cooking tonight, it was really good." Put phones away for 20 minutes of real talk each evening.
Week 3
Something new
Do one activity neither of you has done: a new hiking trail, a cooking class, a different neighbourhood, a museum, a sport. Take turns choosing.
Week 4
Your own lives
Each person spends time on their own friends or hobby, then shares stories with the other. Then plan the next month together.

body: You do not need expensive trips. New does not mean costly. It means different from your usual routine.
Other ideas that help many couples:

ul: Ask questions you have never asked: "What's something you want to try in the next year?"
Look at old photos and talk about how you met.
Bring back small affection: a hug when they come home, holding hands on a walk.
Learn how your partner likes to receive love. cv.cm's love language test is a popular framework for this conversation, though research support for it is limited.
Deal with the small hurts you have been avoiding. Distance often hides unspoken problems.

sections.h: Mistakes that make a slump worse

ul: Waiting for it to fix itself while both people drift further apart.
Blaming: "You're boring now" makes a partner defensive, not closer.
Trying to create excitement through jealousy, flirting with others, or testing your partner. These damage trust.
Making huge decisions to escape the feeling, such as moving in, marriage or a baby, hoping it will fix the distance.
Comparing your relationship to the start, or to other couples online.

body: Counselling is not only for couples in crisis. It can help when:

ul: You have tried for a few months and nothing changes.
One of you wants to work on it and the other does not engage.
Contempt, constant criticism or long silences have become normal.
There has been a betrayal, such as an affair, that you cannot get past.
You cannot talk about the problem without it turning into a fight.

body: A slump is about distance, not fear. If you feel afraid of your partner, or they control your money, phone or friends, that is not a slump. Couples counselling is often not advised in that case; contact a domestic violence service where you live, or local emergency services if you are in danger.

faq.q: How long does a relationship slump last?
faq.a: There is no fixed length. Some last a few weeks, others months. It usually gets shorter when both partners notice it and make changes together.

faq.q: Is it normal to feel bored in a long relationship?
faq.a: Yes. The intense excitement of the first months fades for almost everyone. Boredom is a signal to add new shared experiences, not proof that love is gone.

faq.q: Should we take a break during a slump?
faq.a: A formal break can create uncertainty. Many couples do better with more personal time inside the relationship, plus new things together. If you do take a break, agree on its length and rules.

faq.q: What should I say to my partner if I feel we are in a rut?
faq.a: Start with the wish, not the complaint: "I miss feeling close to you. Can we try something new together this month?" Then ask how they feel.

faq.q: Can a relationship recover from a slump?
faq.a: Yes, many do, especially when both people still respect each other and want to try. Couples often feel closer after working through it.
